analysis.one_liner: Terminates the federal income tax code in 2003 without a replacement, keeping only Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 219-209 on June 17, 1998, but the Senate Finance Committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended every tax collected under the federal income tax code at the end of 2002 — personal income taxes, corporate income taxes, the estate tax, capital gains taxes — while keeping only the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare. It offered no replacement: it merely 'declares' that the new tax system should be simple and fair, and asks Congress to approve one by July 4, 2002. If Congress failed to agree on a new system in time, the federal government would simply lose most of its revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and profitable businesses pay the large majority of income tax under the current code, so repealing it would hand them the largest tax cuts. Advocates of overhauling the tax system — including supporters of a flat tax or national sales tax — would gain the opening to design a replacement. Taxpayers frustrated with filing complexity would be freed from the income tax, at least until a replacement was written.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Internal Revenue Code from imposing any tax for any year beginning after December 31, 2002, ending the personal and corporate income tax, the estate tax, and other taxes under that code.
It preserves the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare, the self-employment tax, and the railroad retirement tax, so those programs' dedicated funding streams continue.

The bill declares that any replacement system should apply a low rate to all Americans, provide tax relief for working Americans, eliminate the bias against savings and investment, and not penalize marriage or families.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would lose most of its revenue — the income tax supplies the majority of federal funding, paying for defense, Medicaid, veterans' benefits, federal pensions, and interest on the debt. Whoever would have paid a replacement tax (the bill names none) would bear the burden, and if Congress failed to pass one by its own deadline of July 4, 2002, deep spending cuts or unprecedented deficits would follow.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the tax code without enacting a replacement — it only 'declares' that a new system should exist and asks Congress to approve one by July 4, 2002, with no mechanism forcing that to happen.

If no replacement was approved by the deadline, the federal government would have no income tax revenue at all, forcing either massive spending cuts or new borrowing; the bill creates a revenue cliff with no safety net.

Replacements discussed at the time, such as a national sales tax, tend to fall proportionally harder on lower- and middle-income families, who spend nearly all their income, than on high earners who save and invest — a cost an honest supporter of repeal would have to acknowledge.

Repealing the income tax would also wipe out provisions many families rely on, such as the child credit, the earned income tax credit, and the charitable and mortgage-interest deductions, unless the unpassed replacement re-created them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The income tax is genuinely complex and its annual filing burden is real, but this bill was not a workable reform: it repealed more than half of federal revenue on a deadline without passing any replacement, leaving the entire burden of designing one to a future Congress that had already failed to agree on one. It functioned as a political statement against the tax code rather than a complete tax plan, and its risks fell hardest on the federal programs and services ordinary people depend on.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill 219-209, but it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Largent introduced the Tax Code Termination Act on January 27, 1998, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
The bill gathered 153 cosponsors — 147 Republicans and 6 Democrats.
The House leadership brought the bill to the floor on June 17, 1998 under a closed rule that barred amendments, and the House passed it 219-209, with 204 Republicans and only 15 Democrats in favor.

Before passage, Democrats offered a motion to recommit the bill with instructions to report a substitute expressing the sense of Congress that comprehensive tax reform should be enacted by April 15, 2001, with hearings within 30 days; it failed 203-223, with 196 of 206 Democrats supporting it and 6 of 226 Republicans.
The amended version passed by the House extended the termination date from 2001 to the end of 2002 and added the July 4, 2002 deadline for Congress to approve a replacement system.
The Senate received the bill on June 18, 1998 and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people who came out ahead were those who rely on federally funded programs — defense, Medicaid, veterans' benefits, and other services paid for by the income tax — since the code was never repealed and its revenue stream continued. The existing tax system, with its deductions and credits, also survived intact for another Congress to reform through ordinary legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal programs funded by income taxes

sides.party_line_note: The vote split sharply by party: 204 of 227 Republicans voted for the bill while only 15 of 206 Democrats did, and on the Democrats' motion to recommit, 196 of 206 Democrats supported it against 6 of 226 Republicans.

industries.note: High earners pay the largest share of income tax, so repealing the code would deliver them the biggest windfall — while the bill specified no replacement that would preserve progressivity, and a consumption-based replacement would shift the burden toward ordinary working families.
The bill ends the corporate income tax and the estate and gift taxes, eliminating the taxes businesses and large estates pay; whatever replacement tax Congress wrote later would fall on someone else.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax would erase the multibillion-dollar annual market in tax filing services and software built on the code's complexity. The industry's interest in keeping the code aligned with the public only insofar as the bill's repeal-without-replacement design was risky for everyone.
Repealing the income tax removes the charitable deduction that encourages giving to nonprofits; unless an unpassed replacement re-created it, donations would likely fall.

The bill would have created a revenue cliff that forced either deep cuts in federal spending or new borrowing, threatening contractors and providers who deliver government-funded services — but only if Congress failed to pass a replacement by its own deadline.
